title: chaotic-burst-recovery-prober-for-dedicated-capacity
creator: Aisha Patel
description: Build a repeatable, automated 'chaotic burst' prober that validates Dedicated capacity autoscaling and steady-state stability under mixed workloads. The prober will inject randomized microbursts on top of a baseline steady tokens/sec workload, measure p95 and tail-latency, detect oscillations, and surface regressions versus a stored baseline. This ticket covers harness implementation, metric collection, dashboards, a reproducible job definition for the dedicated canary pool, and a regression-alerting rule integrated with the existing test-signal pipeline.
background: We currently run deterministic soak and burst scenarios, but a gap remains: production often exhibits irregular microbursts layered over steady traffic. Those patterns reveal autoscaler ramp latencies and oscillation vulnerabilities that our existing tests (fixed-duration bursts + long soaks) do not exercise. Prior tickets covered canonical burst+soak patterns but not chaotic mixes or regression alerting tied to a historical baseline.
acceptance_criteria: A reproducible Kubernetes job (k8s Job manifest) named 'chaos-burst-prober' that can run against the Dedicated canary pool and the staging runtime
Prober produces time-series: tokens/sec (per-route), request p95, request p99, queue depth, GPU util, and autoscaler events (scale-up/scale-down timestamps) exported to Prometheus/Billing BigQuery
Automated run: 6-hour baseline steady at 120k tokens/sec with randomized microbursts (durations 10-90s) ramping to 600k tokens/sec peak, repeatable seedable RNG
Regression detection rule: raise alert if p95 increases >15% and absolute p95 > 250ms over baseline for a 10m sliding window
Autoscaler SLO: time-to-scale (from sustained overload to target capacity) must be <= 90s for <=3x sustained load spikes, and no scaling flaps >3 within 30m after a successful scale-up
Test run artifacts: stored logs, Grafana dashboard link, and a sign-off comment from runtime on-call that no stability regressions were observed in the canary pool run
Playbook snippet added to the Dedicated runbook describing how to re-run the prober, interpret alerts, and rollback model variant/route config if needed
steps: Design phase: define microburst generator parameters (amplitude, duration distribution, inter-arrival distribution) and prompt-length mix to exercise KV cache and different kernel paths
Implement prober harness in Go (based on existing soak runner) with pluggable workload profile and RNG seed support
Add instrumentation hooks to emit autoscaler events and queue depth metrics to Prometheus; ensure token accounting aligns with billing metrics
Create k8s Job and CI job for nightly canary runs; add parameters to target dedicated canary pool namespace
Build Grafana dashboard with baseline overlay and an alert panel for p95 regression detection; add a Prometheus alert rule that triggers CI/regression pipeline
Run initial canary: 6h run, capture artifacts, analyze p95 drift and scale timings
Iterate on thresholds and synthetic workload shapes based on initial findings; document compromises (e.g., increased KV warmup vs. steady-state fairness)
Ship playbook and mark ticket Done after two consecutive nightly passes with no regression alerts
implementation_notes: Use existing soak-runner library but refactor workload generator into a strategy interface; avoid duplicating token accounting logic
Workload profile should include 60% short prompts (<=64 tokens), 30% mid (65-512), 10% long (>512) to exercise both attention and KV-cache behavior
Microburst distribution: Pareto for heavy tails with configurable min/max and average target multiplier
Ensure warmup period (20m) at baseline before first burst to stabilize caches; record separate pre-burst baseline snapshot
Fallback testing: when capacity unavailable, validate automated fallback to quantized model variant and record delta in p95 and token cost
Telemetry: correlate autoscaler events with GPU utilization and queue depth to explain scale decisions
Avoid running on production pools; use dedicated-canary-1 and dedicated-canary-2 namespaces
risks_and_tradeoffs: Running aggressive microbursts in shared test clusters could affect other QA jobs—mitigation: isolate to canary pool and schedule during off-peak windows
Tight p95 thresholds may generate false positives due to transient infra noise—mitigation: use sliding-window and require sustained deviation
Caveat: KV cache warmup is non-linear; a test that warms cache artificially may hide cold-start regressions. We keep an explicit cold-start job variant to track that separately
Quantized fallback validation increases test complexity but is necessary to validate graceful degradation under capacity constraints
